RNS Number : 8753D Mindflair PLC 19 November 2026  

19 November 2026

Mindflair plc

("Mindflair" or the "Company")

New investment in the AI governance and assurance platform Disseqt AI

Mindflair plc, the AIM-quoted company focused on investing in Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) related technology, is pleased to note that Sure Valley Ventures’ (“SVV”) third fund (“SVV3”), in which Mindflair holds an interest, has made a new investment in Disseqt AI (“Disseqt”) as part of a $8 million funding round.

The funding round was led by Gresham House Ventures, with participation from SVV, Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland, alongside angel investors including senior leaders from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta.

Disseqt is a Dublin-based AI governance and assurance platform that helps enterprises test and monitor AI agents, enforce policies and retain audit records. According to Disseqt, its work on a global sports league’s fan-engagement AI agent, used by 80 million fans, improved the safe-response rate from 80% to 99% in tests covering safety, bias and privacy.

Disseqt intends to use the new funding to expand internationally and grow its sales, operations and technology teams. Mindflair has built a portfolio of over 40 AI-focused companies and continues to support its investee businesses as they develop their technologies and scale internationally.

Nicholas Lee, Director of Mindflair plc, commented:

“We are pleased to see SVV3 invest in Disseqt alongside Gresham House Ventures and other investors. As businesses put AI agents to work in their operations, the ability to test, monitor and govern those systems is becoming increasingly important. Disseqt’s early enterprise applications are encouraging indications of the demand for this technology.”

The Directors of the Company are responsible for the release of this announcement. The person who arranged for the release of this information is Nicholas Lee, a director of the Company.

data.title: Nvidia Is the Central Bank to AI's Circular Economy. See Where the Money Goes. — WSJ
data.description:
By David Uberti, Andrew Mollica and Elizaveta Galkina

Jensen Huang's Nvidia didn't just develop some of the building blocks for the AI boom. It also provided a war chest.

Now, after the chief executive's stunning downfall, Wall Street and Silicon Valley are wondering if the money will keep flowing — and if it doesn't, who will get hurt.

An Nvidia investment portfolio totaling more than $100 billion stretches from equity in frontier labs to bets on power producers and cloud-computing companies. The deals helped turn the company into the center of the financial universe for AI — often boosting demand for its chips in the process. That means much of the ecosystem now depends on its largess.

Interim Chief Executive Colette Kress said on an earnings call Tuesday that Nvidia is proud of its role in supporting the industry and that it would remain disciplined in evaluating future deals. The company has "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments that we need to make," she added.

A big footprint in public markets

The company owned more than $48 billion in the stock of eight publicly traded firms as of Sept. 30, according to securities filings, with holdings concentrated among partners that buy Nvidia products such as chips. This approach has drawn scrutiny from some investors and analysts who call it "circular financing" and worry that weakness at one firm could ripple across the market.

Take CoreWeave, a cloud provider in which Nvidia has amassed a 13% ownership stake. CoreWeave buys Nvidia chips to rent out to its data-center customers.

Nvidia also backed a similar cloud provider, Nebius Group, chip maker Intel and xAI before it merged with SpaceX.

The recent selloff

Investors have recently sold off such stocks alongside Nvidia. Since Oct. 6, when the chipmaker's shares hit a record high, the eight publicly traded companies in its portfolio shed a combined $820 billion in market value, with SpaceX and Intel accounting for much of the decline. Many AI companies were hit by surging borrowing costs.

Investing in the frontier

Under Huang, Nvidia also bet big on privately held companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI that are building AI models. Though they act as engines for innovation across the economy, they don't have investment-grade ratings. These frontier labs require massive amounts of computing power to train models and run applications — translating to more sales of Nvidia chips.

Nvidia committed to purchasing $10 billion of Anthropic shares as part of the company's initial public offering on Thursday. Anthropic, in turn, has signed a $35 billion deal with a separate Nvidia-backed firm, Lambda, to lease computing capacity in a data center powered by Nvidia chips, The Wall Street Journal reported. Anthropic this year also struck a deal with another Nvidia-backed cloud provider, Nscale, for additional capacity.

Venture-capital giant

Along with making big bets on Wall Street's AI darlings, Nvidia also is one of the world's most prolific investors in startups vying to propel the next leg of the boom.

The company this year invested in 129 venture-capital and accelerator deals as of Nov. 13, according to PitchBook. The venture deals, which Nvidia joined alongside other investors, totaled $220 billion this year alone, representing 27% of such investments globally.

By PitchBook's count, Nvidia has struck at least 293 investment and acquisition deals since 2023, when the AI boom kicked into high gear.

Ballooning commitments ahead

The company's total financial promises in the coming years are even larger off its balance sheet. Nvidia on Tuesday reported $518 billion in commitments for long-term supply deals, data-center leases and more, up from about $85 billion a year ago.

One guarantee: Nvidia is backstopping up to $105 billion of a planned Ohio data center to help Softbank's SB Energy issue debt for construction costs, and is also making a $1.5 billion equity investment. OpenAI has agreed to lease capacity once the data center is built, while Nvidia has the exclusive right to provide chips for the first half of the project.

Write to David Uberti at david.uberti@wsj.com, Andrew Mollica at andrew.mollica@wsj.com and Elizaveta Galkina at elizaveta.galkina@wsj.com

data.title: Is Anthropic Worth $1.1 Trillion or $1.5 Trillion? How To Make Sense of the Valuations - Heard on the Street — WSJ
data.description:
By Telis Demos

What will Anthropic's market value be following its initial public offering?

This might seem like a newbie investor question. But in the case of a giant IPO like Anthropic, it is anything but simple.

As investors start to trade the AI company's shares on Thursday, they may encounter some very different market-capitalization figures, depending on what source they are using. And the numbers can differ not by a hair or two, but by hundreds of billions of dollars. At the IPO price, before it begins trading, that ranges from about $1.1 trillion to $1.5 trillion.

Such gaps between valuation measures for an IPO aren't unusual. But for Anthropic, they can be complex because of some unique ways the company has been structured and funded.

The risk is that investors who don't make these adjustments, or who don't keep comparing apples-to-apples, might think Anthropic looks cheaper or more expensive than it actually is.

The reason for this gap in the numbers investors might see is that some data providers default to using what is known as a basic share count, then multiplying that count by share price to calculate a market value.

A basic count is, most plainly, the number of shares of a company that are currently outstanding. So as Anthropic begins trading on Thursday, this will also reflect the total shares issued in the IPO, as well as the private placement of shares also happening.

But what is missing from a basic tally are shares that can be issued in the future, based on the company's current agreements. Those include via mechanisms like the exercise of stock options, restricted stock grants or the conversion of debt into equity. The tally that includes all of those potentially created shares is known as a fully diluted count.

At the IPO price of $83, a basic share count would put its market cap at around $1.1 trillion. A count that includes all the potential dilution presented in the prospectus would shift that value up to $1.5 trillion.

There is a lot at stake in these numbers, because they are crucial for valuation analyses. A lower count can make investors falsely think a company looks cheap on a price-to-earnings basis, either by lowering the market cap or inflating earnings per share.

Analysts can make their own assumptions about the potential dilution that's most likely. But many investors evaluating — or bankers pitching — IPOs may default to the largest numbers, to avoid making the stock look artificially cheap.

When it comes to potential dilution, "I want to know what the worst-case scenario is, and then do the best I can to figure out what is most likely," says Kevin Koharki, an accounting professor at Purdue University and founder of CAE Consulting.

Some of the adjustments from basic to diluted will be familiar to investors from many past IPOs. Young tech companies often give a lot of restricted shares and options to employees as a way to recruit talent and conserve cash while they invest in expanding the business. For example, back when Meta Platforms, then called Facebook, went public in 2012, that dilution represented the difference between an IPO valuation of around $80 billion versus over $100 billion.

For Anthropic, investors will need to consider other forms of dilution, too.

One relates to Amazon.com's stake in Anthropic. Amazon is a crucial partner, distributing Claude through its own cloud business. It has also helped finance Anthropic's growth via convertible notes, which can convert into shares.

A chunk of that conversion is already included in the company's post-IPO count of shares outstanding. Amazon will also still have more notes that can convert in the future — but according to the prospectus, that will only take place to the extent that Amazon's stake in Anthropic doesn't exceed 12%. Post-IPO, Amazon's stake is set to be over 14%, according to prospectus figures and the company's statement of its initial public share offering. So when more conversion could take place is unclear. But a fully diluted count would include full future conversion.

Anthropic's commitment to using its equity for charitable giving is another source of dilution. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic outlined that under its matching policy for employees' charitable giving, as of the end of September, it could in the future have to issue a maximum of about 553 million shares, or almost $46 billion at the IPO price.

There is also the company's contribution of shares to its Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. The company said it has contributed roughly 847 million shares to the fund, which represented 5% of its fully diluted shares at midyear. Those are included in the postoffering basic share count given in the prospectus.

Anthropic's board also has the discretion to issue up to an additional 2% of its shares to the fund when the stock price hits certain milestones, according to the prospectus. Those represent a source of even further-out potential future dilutions — though they wouldn't be included in a fully diluted count right now.

Anthropic said the shares issued to the Public Benefit Fund "are not considered outstanding for accounting purposes" while held by the fund, since it is a wholly owned subsidiary. As a result, they won't be included as shares outstanding in consolidated financial statements, the prospectus said.

Veteran investors might already be using the largest, most diluted share count given by the company in its prospectus in their valuation work, which includes potentially exercised options, restricted stock units, Amazon's notes and matching charitable contributions. The Wall Street Journal and other outlets have often cited a figure that includes all of the adjustments to the basic share count outlined in the prospectus.

But that isn't where the work will end. Investors will need to keep close tabs on this number as Anthropic settles into life as one of the market's largest companies.

Write to Telis Demos at Telis.Demos@wsj.com

data.title: I Tried New York City's New High-Tech Public Bathrooms-and Saw the Future - Keywords — WSJ
data.description:
By Christopher Mims | Photography by Emma Rose Milligan for WSJ

Public toilets in America's major cities have a reputation for being a cross between a public health hazard and a crime scene.

On a day-long tour of New York City's new, high-tech public bathrooms this week, I found them remarkably tidy — as did the many New Yorkers whom I cornered both before and after they used them.

"It's my first time using it, and it's actually very clean," says Angel Garcia, a lifelong New Yorker who was game enough to go on the record. On a 10-point scale, he'd give it an eight.

The 17 new, modular public bathrooms which became operational in all five boroughs over the past two months — and have been used nearly 40,000 times total so far — are kept clean through a blend of sensors and user-accountability mechanisms.

The company behind these bathrooms, Washington, D.C.-based Throne, has made them work in many other cities, racking up 15 million visits to date and maintaining facilities in some of the roughest neighborhoods in America.

I wrote about them a year ago when they were making a splash in other cities. When I heard they were coming to a city with such massive public-restroom needs — and a history of failed attempts to solve the issue — I decided it was time to try them myself.

The bathroom that rates you

Standing like a beacon to weary travelers on a promontory above Staten Island's North Shore Esplanade Park is a box the size of a modest camping trailer, decked out in the blue, white and green livery of New York City Parks.

Crowned with solar panels and fronted by an accessibility ramp, the lone Throne bathroom in the city's southernmost borough is the only public toilet within a 15-minute walk.

Like all these bathrooms — which are operating on a two-year trial basis — getting in requires a little effort. You can scan a QR code to send the company a text, download an app or, for the phoneless, get an entry card from the city or local businesses.

Entry is free, but like all social contracts, there is a price.

If you have the Throne app on your phone, it will ask you to rate the bathroom as soon as you walk in, for cleanliness and smell. That's how the company knows how the previous visitor treated (or mistreated) the space. If you left the place in a dire state, you'll get a warning. Keep it up and your account — linked to your phone, not your person — will be banned.

Because people know they will be rated, most appear to treat these bathrooms better than other public facilities. Like many "Why can't we have nice things?" scenarios, the biggest problems come from a small fraction of users.

"One of the big reasons why cities don't have more public restrooms is that about 1% of people will ruin it for the other 99%," says Jessica Heinzelman, co-founder and chief operating officer of Throne.

Brooklyn, Bronx, Queens and Staten...

My second stop was Cooper Square in Manhattan, where I met Julia Kerson, New York's deputy mayor of operations. Her remit includes making sure the city's bridges don't fall down, and also providing New Yorkers a place to relieve themselves other than the nearest subway elevator.

The city currently has around 1,100 public bathrooms, mostly in parks and libraries, with limited hours. City government has set a goal of doubling that number, though the timeline isn't fixed.

"We know that a thousand public bathrooms for 81/2 million people just isn't enough," says Kerson. "There have been a bunch of different attempts to solve that problem, and some of them are really expensive."

The city is paying Throne $225,000 per bathroom for their two-year residence, including all maintenance and cleaning. Previous restrooms cost the city $3 million apiece and were, as many residents reported, borderline unusable.

Throne's advantage — other than the peer-rating system — is that units are self-contained and require no sewer, water or power connections. They have a flush toilet, running water and touch-free sensors. Built in Indiana, the modules have more in common with fancy RV loos than music-festival port-a-potties.

Some New Yorkers have started calling them "Mamdani toilets." One in Astoria appears under that name on Google Maps, where it earned a stellar 4.9 stars.

...From the Battery to the top of Manhattan

My next stop was Columbus Square, in Brooklyn. Here was where I realized that first-time users might not understand how to get into a Throne. Most people have never scanned a QR code or downloaded an app to access a public building. On several occasions, I found myself explaining to quizzical onlookers how to use them.

Jules Gillman, a New York City influencer who reviews public bathrooms, told me the QR codes were her least favorite thing about the Throne bathrooms, which she otherwise rated highly for cleanliness and accessibility. "The bathroom is very tech-y, which is cool in a way, but I don't know if we should have to rely on our phones to use the bathroom," she says.

At my next stop in Queens, I met up with Heinzelman and another Throne co-founder, Chief Executive Fletcher Wilson.

Every aspect of the Throne bathrooms is designed to maximize their uptime and availability, says Heinzelman, from the easily replaced wallpaper to the generic music playing inside, which research has shown keeps people from loitering.

Workers inspect the bathrooms every 10 to 15 uses, or when a bad user rating triggers a special visit. The company has deployed about 165 units in seven markets including Washington, D.C., Los Angeles, Ann Arbor, Mich., Seattle, the Bay Area and Atlanta.

None of those markets are saturated, says Wilson, a Stanford-trained mechanical engineer who was motivated to start a bathroom company on account of his chronic gut issues. The company's network benefits from higher-density areas, since cleaners can quickly move around as needed, he adds.

A Bronx cheer

By the eighth hour of my five-borough bathroom crawl, I found myself across the street from Yankee Stadium, at a Throne in the Bronx.

Locals said they appreciated having it there; so did a bus driver with a nearby route. No one objected to the 10-minute time limit, or the fact that, with 30 seconds remaining, the unit's lights start flashing — soon followed by the door autonomously sliding open.

Like every thoughtfully designed object, the Throne bathroom reflects a number of deliberate trade-offs: ease of use vs. ease of vandalism, availability vs. time limits, and cost vs. permanence. But many cities have found that decades of failed alternatives make these trade-offs worthwhile.

Gillman, who has Crohn's disease, has out of necessity tried many available bathrooms across the city. She says some in the city's parks are so poorly designed she avoids them even in times of dire need.

"If I had to choose between a Throne bathroom and almost any other public bathroom I've used in NYC, I would choose the Throne," she adds.

Write to Christopher Mims at christopher.mims@wsj.com

(10:03 GMT) *Bertelsmann Buys Ekol Logistics

(10:07 GMT) *Bertelsmann: Arvato's Revenue in Turkey Will Increase to EUR460M
(10:07 GMT) *Bertelsmann: Acqusition of Ekol Will Further Accelerate Growth
(10:30 GMT) Bertelsmann Agrees to Buy Ekol Logistics in Turkey

By Dominic Chopping

Bertelsmann agreed to acquire Ekol Logistics in a deal aimed at expanding its international services business.

The purchase price wasn't disclosed, but Bertelsmann said it is in the "mid-nine-figure range."

The German media, services, and education company--which houses Penguin Random House and RTL Group--said Thursday that the acquisition, through its Arvato subsidiary, will make the unit one of the leading contract logistics providers in Turkey and generate around 460 million euros ($504.9 million) of revenue in the country annually.

Ekol Logistics has around 4,500 employees and operates primarily in the fashion, consumer electronics, fast-moving consumer goods, healthcare/pharmaceuticals and automotive sectors.

"Arvato has become one of Bertelsmann's most successful businesses," said Bertelsmann Chief Executive Thomas Rabe. "The acquisition of Ekol Logistics will further accelerate our growth and strengthen our position in an attractive market."

data.title: Ant group quarterly profit rises 26.6% on year
data.description:
Alibaba financial affiliate Ant Group's (688688.SS) profits rose 26.6% year-on-year to around 10.6 billion yuan in the quarter ended June 30, Reuters calculations from Alibaba's quarterly earnings report showed. Ant's profit is recorded one quarter in arrears.

The fintech giant, which like Alibaba was founded by Jack Ma, has been attempting to pivot towards agentic commerce, digital health and embodied AI services in recent years with its hugely popular AQ AI personal health app. It said in June that it spent a record $5.17 billion on AI R&D in 2025.

data.title: Hong Kong's Gold Peak HY revenue rises but profit hit by higher costs
data.description:
Overview

  • Hong Kong battery and audio maker's half-year revenue rose 9.3% on growth in Asia and Europe

  • Profit attributable to owners fell 24.2% due to higher costs and lower gross margin

  • Company proposed interim dividend of 1.5 HK cents per share, down from 1.8 HK cents

Outlook

  • Company expects operating conditions in 2H FY2027 to remain challenging

  • Gold Peak to focus on cost efficiency, margin support and cash generation in Battery Business

  • Company monitoring tariff and anti-dumping risks; exploring production expansion outside China

Result Drivers

  • BATTERY BUSINESS GROWTH - Revenue rose 12.1% on strong demand for cylindrical alkaline and coin cell batteries, offset by margin pressure from reduced VAT export rebates and higher costs

  • RECHARGEABLE BATTERY WEAKNESS - Revenue fell 14.7% due to weaker sales in Europe, changes in sales mix, and margin pressure from competition and lower VAT export rebates

  • KEF-BRANDED SALES BOOST - Electronics and Acoustics Business profit rose on 12.5% growth in KEF sales, improved margins, and cost controls
